Moral Foundations Theory is a framework that separates human morality into the following categories:

  - Care/Harm: related to our long evolution as mammals with attachment systems
    and an ability to feel (and dislike) the pain of others. It underlies the
    virtues of kindness, gentleness, and nurturance.

  - Loyalty/Betrayal: related to our long history as tribal creatures able to
    form shifting coalitions. It is active anytime people feel that it is "one
    for all and all for one." It underlies the virtues of patriotism and
    self-sacrifice for the group.

  - Authority/Subversion: shaped by our long primate history of hierarchical
    social interactions. It underlies virtues of leadership and followership,
    including deference to prestigious authority figures and respect for
    traditions.

  - Sanctity/Purity: shaped by the psychology of disgust and contamination. It
    underlies notions of striving to live in an elevated, less carnal, more
    noble, and more "natural" way (often present in religious narratives). This
    foundation underlies the widespread idea that the body is a temple that can
    be desecrated by immoral activities and contaminants (an idea not unique to
    religious traditions). It underlies the virtues of self-discipline,
    self-improvement, naturalness, and spirituality.

  - Equality: related to our intuitions about equal treatment and equal outcome
    for individuals.

  - Proportionality: related to our intuitions about individuals getting
    rewarded in proportion to their merit or contribution.

# Labour Party Manifesto 2005 Summary

## Overview and Vision

The 2005 Labour Manifesto, titled "Britain Forward, Not Back," presents New Labour's plan for a third term, built on the principle that government must provide opportunity and security for all in a changing world. The foreword, written as a personal message from the party leader, reflects on achievements since 1997—economic stability, improved public services, and reduced poverty—while acknowledging difficult decisions made, including on Iraq.

## Economic Record and Plans

Labour claims unprecedented economic success: the longest period of uninterrupted growth in modern history, lowest sustained interest rates for a generation, and two million more people in work since 1997. The manifesto commits to maintaining economic stability through continued Bank of England independence, keeping inflation at two percent, and borrowing only to invest.

Key economic pledges include not raising basic or top income tax rates, raising the minimum wage to £5.35 by October 2006, and aiming for an 80 percent employment rate. The party promises to reform Incapacity Benefit and continue welfare-to-work programmes while supporting enterprise through reduced regulation and investment in science and innovation.

## Education

Education remains "number one priority." The manifesto celebrates improved primary school results, with ten-year-olds ranked third globally in literacy. Plans include making every secondary school an independent specialist school, expanding the Academies programme to 200 schools by 2010, and introducing specialised vocational diplomas for 14-19 year-olds.

Investment in education will continue rising as a share of national income. The manifesto commits to 50 percent of young people attending higher education by 2010 and caps tuition fees at £3,000 (inflation-adjusted) for the entire Parliament.

## Healthcare

NHS spending has doubled since 1997 and will triple by 2008. The manifesto celebrates 27,000 additional doctors and 79,000 more nurses, with waiting times dramatically reduced. Future commitments include eliminating waits over 18 weeks from referral to treatment by 2008, offering patients free choice of hospital, and tackling MRSA through improved hygiene standards.

Public health initiatives include banning high-fat foods from school meals, restricting advertising of unhealthy foods to children, and implementing smokefree legislation in enclosed public places and workplaces, with exemptions for some pubs and membership clubs.

## Crime and Security

The manifesto claims crime has fallen 30 percent since 1997. Key pledges include a neighbourhood policing team for every community, expanding Community Support Officers to 24,000, and introducing compulsory drug testing for property and drug offenders. Anti-social behaviour measures will be strengthened, and ID cards with biometric data will be introduced voluntarily as people renew passports.

On immigration, a points-based system will be established prioritizing skilled workers, with fingerprinting for visa applicants and electronic border tracking within five years.

## Families and Welfare

The manifesto commits to ending child poverty, starting by halving it by 2010-11. Paid maternity leave will increase to nine months by 2007, aiming for twelve months by Parliament's end. Universal childcare will be established with 3,500 Sure Start Children's Centres by 2010, and homeownership will increase by another one to two million.

## International Policy

Labour pledges continued EU leadership, putting the Constitutional Treaty to referendum. On defence, the party commits to maintaining the independent nuclear deterrent while modernizing armed forces. The manifesto acknowledges Iraq War controversies while calling for unity in supporting Iraqi democracy.

Climate change and African poverty are highlighted as G8 presidency priorities, with commitment to reaching 0.7 percent of national income for development aid by 2013.

## Constitutional Reform

Promises include completing House of Lords reform, devolving more power to local authorities, and enhancing Welsh Assembly powers. The manifesto defends the Human Rights Act while promising to address "abusive or frivolous claims" and establish a Commission on Equality and Human Rights.

# Summary of UKIP Manifesto 2005

## Core Mission

The UK Independence Party's 2005 manifesto centres on one fundamental objective: withdrawing Britain from the European Union to restore sovereignty to Westminster. Party leader Roger Knapman argues that Brussels effectively governs Britain, and no domestic issues can be properly addressed while EU membership continues. The party views the EU as undemocratic, corrupt, and unreformable.

## Withdrawal Process

UKIP proposed repealing the 1972 European Communities Act to achieve formal withdrawal, immediately stopping EU budget contributions and resuming independent participation in international bodies like the World Trade Organisation. A two-year transition period would manage the replacement of EU-originated laws with British alternatives.

## Economic Policies

**Trade:** The party expressed confidence that trade with European neighbours would continue post-withdrawal, noting Britain buys more from EU countries than it sells. They proposed bilateral trade agreements similar to Switzerland's arrangement and strengthening links with Commonwealth nations, NAFTA countries, and the Far East.

**Regulation:** UKIP promised wholesale deregulation, particularly for small businesses employing fewer than twenty people. They argued EU regulations add costs and damage employment, with the presumption being that regulations should be scrapped unless overwhelmingly justified.

**Budget and Taxation:** The party proposed using Britain's approximately £12 billion annual EU contribution to raise state pensions by £25 per week. They advocated halving council taxes, scrapping the 10% income tax bracket, raising inheritance tax thresholds to £500,000, and reinstating pension fund tax credits. Long-term goals included implementing a flat tax system and replacing VAT with a wholesale-point sales tax.

## Public Services

**NHS:** UKIP criticised centralised management and performance targets, proposing to remove government from day-to-day NHS management, return to the matron system, restore hospital control to local boards, and allow GPs professional autonomy.

**Education:** The party advocated greater school autonomy, scrapping Standard Aptitude Tests, empowering headteachers over exclusions, and introducing assisted-places schemes for private education. They criticised university expansion, proposing to withdraw funding from substandard courses and cancel top-up fees.

**Pensions:** Besides the £25 weekly increase, UKIP promised to reinstate dividend tax credits for pension funds and restore rights for expatriate pensioners with frozen pensions.

## Home Affairs

**Law and Order:** Proposals included credible minimum prison sentences, strengthening magistrates' powers, reducing police paperwork, making Chief Constables locally accountable, and building new prisons as required.

**Immigration:** UKIP advocated approaching zero net immigration through a points-based work permit system, reinstating embarkation controls, introducing "Britishness" tests, setting independent refugee criteria, and requiring health checks for immigrants.

## Agriculture and Fisheries

The party promised to replace CAP subsidies with guaranteed minimum prices, protect farmers from supermarket buying power, and reward environmentally-friendly farming. For fishing, they proposed re-establishing British control over coastal waters and implementing conservation zones.

## Defence and Foreign Policy

UKIP advocated reversing military cuts, withdrawing from EU common defence plans, maintaining NATO membership while preserving independent action capability, and buying British-made equipment where possible.

## Other Policies

**Energy:** The party opposed wind power development and supported nuclear power expansion and clean coal technology.

**Environment:** They proposed British-controlled environmental legislation, opposing GM crops until proven safe.

**Governance:** UKIP supported maintaining the House of Lords, introducing referendums triggered by 5% of the electorate petitioning, scrapping English regional assemblies, and restoring local council autonomy with business rates returned to local control.

## Conclusion

The manifesto concluded by criticising the regulatory, dependency, and compensation cultures fostered by EU membership and excessive state control. UKIP proposed repealing the Human Rights Act, dropping identity card plans, and repealing the Hunting Act, envisioning a deregulated, prosperous Britain with restored traditional values.
